title: Life-sustaining cryobanking of human-scale organs

concept.text: The innovation is a reliable way to bank whole human-scale solid organs at cryogenic temperatures, then recover them for transplantation with function sufficient to sustain a recipient. Its defining capability would be an inventory of transplantable organs maintained for months or years, with acceptable injury after recovery and durable graft function after implantation. Human-scale life-sustaining recovery remains a goal in the supplied evidence.

The approach combines vitrification and nanowarming. Cryoprotectants help an organ enter a glass-like state during cooling, limiting damaging ice formation. Nanoparticles distributed through the organ’s vasculature generate heat internally during rewarming, addressing the difficulty of warming a large organ uniformly from its surface. Successful banking also requires preserving the organ through cryoprotectant loading and removal, cooling, storage, rewarming and restoration of circulation. Solving the heating problem alone does not establish transplantability.

significance.text: Donor-organ preservation currently imposes severe time constraints, usually measured in hours, although some approaches extend preservation into days. Reliable long-term banking would separate procurement from transplantation: organs could be collected into inventories, matched over time, transported with greater flexibility and implanted after recipient preparation. Scheduled procedures and a broader choice among stored organs would change transplantation from an immediate allocation emergency into a more planned clinical service.

The distinctive advance is the ability to maintain an inventory over months or years. Daytime surgery and wider geographic sharing are already partly enabled by shorter preservation extensions; those benefits alone do not establish the need for cryobanking. Long storage would additionally allow matching decisions to draw on organs procured at different times, rather than only those available during a short preservation window.

Greater use of scarce donor organs is a plausible downstream benefit, rather than a guaranteed direct outcome. Realizing it would require suitable allocation policies, safety assessment, banking infrastructure and clinical adoption. Banking could reduce losses caused by timing and logistics, but it cannot create an organ when no suitable donor exists. It therefore complements approaches that expand organ supply and does not by itself resolve the transplant shortage.

missing_breakthrough.text: The central remaining capability in the supplied studies is reproducible, sustained life-supporting transplantation after cryobanking at human scale. Rat kidneys have met a sole-organ survival endpoint, and a pig-kidney preprint reports human-scale recovery and acute transplant function. The next biological question is whether such large grafts can sustain recipients through the initial injury period, recover adequate filtration and maintain function over time. Urine production or short laboratory perfusion cannot answer that question.

Ice formation, thermal-stress cracking and cryoprotectant injury are distinct barriers. Nanowarming addresses the surface-heating bottleneck, but an organ still needs sufficiently uniform cryoprotectant and nanoparticle delivery and controlled cooling and warming throughout its tissue. Cryoprotectant toxicity and the injury associated with its delivery and removal remain important even when physical preservation appears successful. In the rat study, cryoprotectant damage was identified as the limiting factor for biological and functional recovery under the tested conditions.

Translation also requires acceptable vascular, tubular and filtration outcomes after reperfusion, followed by evidence about chronic tissue injury. Residual injury and reduced filtration in the pig experiments leave those questions open. Clinical-grade reagents and processes are another stated translational requirement. Success with one organ type would establish a starting point; different solid organs would still require their own preservation protocols and functional demonstrations.

current_state.text: A peer-reviewed study published in Nature Communications on June 9, 2023 demonstrated vitrification, storage for 1–100 days and nanowarming of rat kidneys followed by life-sustaining transplantation in male rats. All five nanowarmed syngeneic transplant recipients survived the planned 30-day study after removal of their native kidneys. The grafts therefore supplied the recipients’ renal support. Recovery included initial graft dysfunction followed by normalization of renal function; the result should not be read as immediate, injury-free recovery or as evidence of survival beyond the study endpoint.

The same group’s bioRxiv preprint, posted October 14, 2026, reports recovery of approximately 100-g pig kidneys, about 100 times the mass of the previously nanowarmed rat kidneys. Most kidneys in the perfusion experiments had been stored for 1–7 days. One kidney was stored at −150 °C for 366 days and then evaluated by normothermic perfusion, which circulates fluid through the organ at near-body temperature to assess function. The study reports vascular, metabolic and excretory recovery. The year-long storage result concerns one perfusion-assessed kidney and should not be generalized into a replicated year-long transplantation result.

Separate acute transplantation experiments in that preprint included three nanowarmed pig-kidney grafts, with three grafts per comparison group. The recipients retained their contralateral native kidney, and graft function was followed for 120 minutes in a non-survival experiment. The nanowarmed grafts produced urine immediately after transplantation, but residual injury and reduced filtration remained. These experiments establish surgical feasibility, reperfusion and immediate function under the tested conditions. They did not test whether the grafts could provide sustained, sole-organ renal support, and the preprint explicitly identifies survival transplantation as a required next step.

The supplied October 2026 version is a preprint and was not peer reviewed. The supplied review had complete main-article text for the rat study, but the retained pig-preprint extraction ended during page 50 and its figures were not visually inspected. The explicit methods and results summarized above were available within that extraction. These access limits constrain assessment of the entire preprint without negating the accessible experimental descriptions.

Evidence limitation: the supplied material contains no bounded freshness-search record establishing the field’s complete status as of November 1, 2026. It therefore cannot establish that no separate peer-reviewed pig-study publication, human transplantation or subsequent result existed by that date. Neither supplied study demonstrates human transplantation, and the pig study itself does not demonstrate life-sustaining recipient survival; broader claims of absence remain unresolved.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed initial demonstration: reproducibly preserve human-scale kidneys and at least one other solid organ below the glass transition for at least 30 days, then rewarm them with no detectable ice formation or cracking under prespecified assessments. The protocol should state detection limits and sampling coverage, since thermometry and imaging cannot establish the absolute absence of microscopic ice everywhere. These storage durations and organ requirements are proposed milestones, not established scientific or clinical standards.
completion_criteria.label: Human-scale organs reproducibly rewarmed after 30-day cryostorage without detectable ice or cracking

completion_criteria.text: Proposed functional demonstration: transplant the recovered organs into large animals after removal or elimination of the corresponding native organ function, so that recipient survival and the relevant physiological support depend on the graft. For kidneys, assessment should extend beyond urine production to sustained filtration, recovery from tubular injury and tissue outcomes. Prespecified survival and organ-function outcomes at 30 days should meet defined comparison margins against clinically relevant static cold storage controls. A nonsignificant difference alone would not demonstrate comparability.
completion_criteria.label: Recovered grafts sustain recipients with comparable 30-day survival and function

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reproducibility requirements: use sufficient independent organs and recipients to estimate success and failure rates, report initial dysfunction and unsuccessful recoveries, and reproduce the outcome across independent experimental runs and ultimately other centers. Organ-specific endpoints and comparison margins should be selected before testing. A second solid organ would demonstrate broader applicability, while finite experiments would establish the tested range of organs, sizes, storage conditions and protocols rather than universal applicability.
completion_criteria.label: Independent replication quantifies recovery outcomes and establishes tested applicability limits

completion_criteria.text: Proposed clinical progression: after convincing large-animal survival results and development of clinical-grade processes, an initial human series should demonstrate graft function within a prespecified range accepted for conventionally stored deceased-donor organs. Thirty-day storage and follow-up would be an initial milestone. Establishing the full months-to-years banking concept would additionally require replicated recovery after those longer storage durations and substantially longer follow-up for durable graft function, chronic injury and practical clinical use.
completion_criteria.label: Human grafts meet conventional-storage benchmarks after 30-day storage and follow-up

related_concepts.text: Roster-based synthesis — SUR-02, Destination-therapy solid-organ xenotransplantation: xenotransplantation seeks a durable organ supply from another species, while SUR-03 seeks to preserve available organs until transplantation. The capabilities could complement each other if suitable xenografts could also be banked, but that combination would need direct testing. Cryobanking does not resolve the biological barriers to durable xenograft function.

Roster-based synthesis — SUR-12, Life-sustaining autologous solid organs assembled for implantation: SUR-12 addresses creating a patient-derived organ; SUR-03 addresses preserving an organ that already exists. A generated organ might eventually be banked, but preservation compatibility is a separate question. Neither organ assembly nor cryobanking establishes the other capability.

Roster-based synthesis — SUR-01, Operational donor-specific tolerance for the transplants patients actually receive: tolerance addresses the recipient’s immune relationship with a graft, whereas cryobanking addresses preservation and recovery. A well-preserved graft would still require an appropriate immune-management strategy. The syngeneic rat result, obtained between genetically matched animals, does not demonstrate donor-specific tolerance in the broader transplant population.

Roster-based synthesis — SUR-08, Reversible metabolic arrest after traumatic exsanguination cardiac arrest: both concepts concern recovering viable biological function after profound interruption of ordinary physiology. Their targets and demonstrations differ: SUR-08 concerns an injured whole patient during emergency rescue, whereas SUR-03 concerns an isolated organ stored cryogenically and subsequently transplanted. Success in organ vitrification would not establish reversible whole-body arrest.

Roster-based synthesis — SUR-09, Living, perfused autologous replacements for complex parts that grafts do not supply: both require preservation of living tissue architecture and circulation. SUR-09 concerns constructing replacements for complex parts, whereas SUR-03 concerns long-term storage and functional recovery of whole solid organs. Any extension of cryobanking to such replacements would require its own evidence.

unresolved_issues: Whether a separate peer-reviewed version of the pig study, any human transplantation result or subsequent relevant evidence existed by November 1, 2026 remains unverified in the supplied material.
Whether human-scale cryobanked kidneys can sustain recipients without native renal support, recover from initial injury and maintain durable function remains unanswered by the supplied pig study.
The single 366-day perfusion result does not establish reproducible year-long banking or transplantation after year-long storage.
The pig-preprint extraction is truncated and its figures were not visually inspected in the supplied review, limiting assessment beyond the accessible text.

Acceptable injury limits, comparison margins, replication requirements, clinical process specifications and longer-term follow-up durations remain to be defined; the proposed milestones are not established standards.
The choice of a second solid organ and the extent to which preservation protocols transfer between organs remain open.
Related-concept relationships are based on roster titles because full specifications of those innovations were not supplied.

brief.title: Donor organs stored for years and ready to transplant
possible: Someone waiting for a transplant could receive an organ from a stored inventory, matched and prepared when needed. Whole organs could remain banked for months or years, then recover enough function to keep a recipient alive.
Protective chemicals would let organs cool into an ice-free, glass-like state. Nanowarming—heating tiny magnetic particles inside the organ’s blood vessels—would warm them evenly from within.
why: Patients and transplant teams could choose among organs donated at different times, instead of racing against a short preservation window. Banking would allow more time for matching, transport and recipient preparation, making transplantation a more planned service.

sources.who: Zonghu Han, Joseph Sushil Rao and colleagues
sources.showed: They recovered rat kidneys after cold storage and nanowarming. Transplants sustained rats without their native kidneys through a 30-day study, despite initial dysfunction.
sources.quote: Full renal function was restored after nanowarming and transplantation, with the transplanted organs sustaining the life of the recipient animals.
sources.cited_for: Stored kidneys can recover enough function after rewarming to sustain a recipient.
sources.not_established: The study did not establish life-sustaining recovery of human-sized organs or durable function beyond its follow-up.

sources.who: Zonghu Han, Bat-Erdene Namsrai and colleagues at the University of Minnesota
sources.showed: This preprint reports recovery of human-sized pig kidneys. They functioned during tests with circulating warm fluid and produced urine immediately after transplantation, although injury and reduced blood filtration remained.
sources.quote:
Rewarmed kidneys demonstrated vascular, metabolic 
and excretory function during normothermic perfusion, with limited histological injury, and 
reperfused homogeneously and produced urine immediately after transplantation.
sources.cited_for: The preservation and rewarming process can recover some function in human-sized kidneys.
sources.not_established: Brief transplant tests with a working native kidney did not establish that the recovered organs could sustain recipients.

shown: Zonghu Han and colleagues demonstrated life-sustaining transplantation of banked rat kidneys. All recipients survived the planned 30-day study without their native kidneys. Kidney function recovered after initial dysfunction.

The same group’s pig-kidney preprint extends recovery to human-sized organs, with immediate urine production after transplantation. A kidney also functioned in a laboratory test after a year in storage. Neither result demonstrates sustained life support at this scale.
missing: Repeated transplants must show that human-sized banked organs can sustain recipients without help from the corresponding native organs.
Preservation must control ice, cracking and chemical injury while allowing lasting recovery of blood flow, filtration and tissue health.
Reliable recovery after months or years, clinical-grade processes and successful human transplantation remain to be demonstrated.

milestones.label: Human-sized organs rewarm without detectable ice or cracks
milestones.explanation: Human-sized kidneys and another solid organ would have to rewarm repeatedly after 30 days in a glass-like state, without ice or cracks under defined detection limits. This would establish physical preservation at the needed scale.

milestones.label: Recovered organs sustain recipients with comparable survival and function
milestones.explanation: Large-animal recipients depending on recovered organs would have to meet predefined survival and function margins against conventional cold storage at 30 days. This would establish life support beyond brief function tests.

milestones.label: Independent replication establishes reliability and tested limits
milestones.explanation: Independent runs and other centers would have to quantify successes and failures across defined conditions, including another solid organ. This would establish reliability and the tested range of applicability.

milestones.label: Human transplants meet conventional storage benchmarks
milestones.explanation: Human organs would have to meet accepted conventional-storage function benchmarks after 30 days of banking and equally long follow-up. This would begin clinical validation; longer banking and follow-up would test durability.

uncertain: Acceptable injury, comparison margins and replication requirements remain undefined; these milestones are proposed goals rather than established standards.
The best choice of another solid organ, and how much of the kidney preservation process would transfer to it, remain open.
Whether human-sized organs can recover from initial injury and maintain adequate function over the long term remains unanswered.

page.title: Cryogenic banking of human solid organs
page.definition: Whole human solid organs are stored in a vitrified state—a solid glass without ice crystals—then rewarmed and transplanted with life-sustaining function. Organs procured at different times can enter the same transplant inventory.

goal.need: U.S. teams usually transplant hearts within 6 hours of recovery, livers within 12 and kidneys within 36. In 2021–2023, more than 60% of unused U.S. donor kidneys had the same recorded reason: the candidate list was exhausted without a recipient being found. Months of storage could let a team compare organs donated at different times, find a suitable match and prepare the patient for surgery. The organ would still need to function after rewarming, and the donor and recipient would still need to be compatible.

completion.title: A cryobanked human solid organ is successfully transplanted into a recipient.
completion.criterion: First successful clinical transplantation of a human kidney, heart or liver recovered after cryopreservation. The roadmap lists these organs separately. It specifies no minimum storage duration, recipient-survival duration, functional cutoff, sample size or replication requirement. These remain limitations of the published completion test.
completion.set_by: Organ Preservation Alliance and New Organ stakeholder roadmapping committee, Beta Roadmap Report, long-term table, item 4. The quoted kidney endpoint has separate counterparts for heart and liver.
completion.threshold_quote: First successful transplantation of banked human kidney
completion.basis: The roadmap places clinical transplantation after large-mammal cryopreservation and pretransplant functional evaluation. This supplies an external clinical endpoint, but leaves successful transplantation operationally undefined. It also supplies no duration requirement establishing months-to-years inventory storage.

milestones.title: A small-mammal solid organ retains physiological function after vitrification and rewarming.
milestones.criterion: Demonstrate an organ-specific physiological function in a whole small-mammal organ after vitrification and rewarming. The roadmap gives no numerical cutoff for the recovered function.
milestones.set_by: Organ Preservation Alliance and New Organ stakeholder roadmapping committee, Beta Roadmap Report, mid-term table, item 2.
milestones.threshold_quote: small mammalian organs with post-thaw functionality

milestones.title: A cryobanked small-mammal organ sustains a recipient without corresponding native-organ support.
milestones.criterion: Transplant the rewarmed organ into a small-mammal recipient whose survival depends on the graft performing that organ’s function. In the kidney model, both native kidneys are removed. The study’s 30-day follow-up is specific to that protocol.
milestones.set_by: Renal cryopreservation research community, using graft-dependent recipient survival; demonstrated explicitly by Han et al. (2023). The published test concerns kidneys.
milestones.threshold_quote: Thus, renal function and survival of the animal depended solely on the transplanted organ.

milestones.title: Vitrified large-mammal organs reliably recover healthy function after rewarming and before transplant.
milestones.criterion: Demonstrate reliable recovery of healthy organ-specific function in rewarmed, vitrified organs of the large-mammal species under study. The roadmap specifies neither a numerical healthy range nor a minimum number or proportion of successful recoveries.
milestones.set_by: Organ Preservation Alliance and New Organ stakeholder roadmapping committee, Beta Roadmap Report, long-term table, item 1.
milestones.threshold_quote: Reliably vitrify large mammalian vital organs with healthy pre-transplant functionality

milestones.title: A cryobanked human-sized organ provides sustained life support in a large-animal recipient.
milestones.criterion: Transplant a rewarmed, cryobanked human-sized organ into a large-animal recipient and demonstrate sustained survival dependent on the graft. For kidneys, this requires follow-up in a recipient without native renal support. The cited large-animal research programme specifies no minimum follow-up or success proportion.
milestones.set_by: Renal cryopreservation research community: Han et al. (2023) establish graft-dependent survival; the University of Minnesota’s report of 6 November 2026 identifies long-term transplantation function as still required. These published tests concern kidneys.
milestones.threshold_quote: Further research is needed to establish long-term function after transplantation

milestones.title: A whole small-mammal organ vitrifies without detectable ice in its tissue.
milestones.criterion: Cool the intact organ below its glass-transition temperature and examine the organ tissue for ice while it remains below that temperature. The tissue itself must show no detectable ice.
milestones.set_by: Whole-organ vitrification convention demonstrated by Fahy and colleagues in a rabbit kidney and identified in the Beta Roadmap Report’s mid-term table, item 2.
milestones.threshold_quote: No ice could be detected in any part of the kidney.

milestones.title: A protocol rapidly assesses a rewarmed human organ’s function before transplantation.
milestones.criterion: Demonstrate a device and protocol for assessing organ-specific function in a whole human donor organ after vitrification and rewarming and before transplantation. The roadmap specifies neither a maximum assessment time nor a numerical functional cutoff.
milestones.set_by: Organ Preservation Alliance and New Organ stakeholder roadmapping committee, Beta Roadmap Report, long-term table, item 3.
milestones.threshold_quote: Devices and protocols for rapid post-thaw, pre-transplant organ assessment

not_found: Targeted FDA, ClinicalTrials.gov and prize searches did not locate a human-organ cryobanking acceptance standard specifying storage duration and graft-survival requirements.
No clinical transplantation of a cryobanked human kidney, heart or liver was located.
No graft-dependent survival transplantation of a cryobanked human-sized kidney, heart or liver was located.
The bioRxiv full text could not be opened; its PMC abstract and the developer’s report were accessible.

No society or programme statement disputing the value or feasibility of banking vitrified human organs for transplantation was located.

results.finding: Eight vitrified pig kidneys recovered excretory function during 120-minute perfusion.
results.detail: Vascular and excretory function remained impaired relative to fresh and cold-stored kidneys, including reduced creatinine clearance. One kidney had been stored for 366 days.
results.quote:
During NMP, VNW kidneys showed prompt, uniform reperfusion and immediate urine 
production (Fig. 3a, Supplementary Video 1). Vascular and excretory function remained 
impaired relative to fresh and 24-h SCS kidneys but was similar to or numerically better than that 
of CPA-only controls (Fig. 3, Extended Data Table 2).

results.finding: Three vitrified pig kidney grafts produced urine during 120-minute acute transplantation experiments.
results.detail: The experiments were non-survival procedures and did not establish sustained life support dependent on the graft.
results.quote:
VNW grafts produced urine immediately after reperfusion and sustained urine production 
throughout the 120-min observation period (Fig. 6b).

results.finding: Whole rat kidneys (at least one imaged per loading condition) had no detectable renal ice on micro-CT at −150 °C.
results.detail: Figure 2 shows representative scans with and without nanoparticles. The text gives n = 8 for the cooling profiles and leaves the total number of kidneys scanned unspecified.
results.quote: These are consistent with successful vitrification of the kidney itself and ice present in the extrarenal fat.

results.finding: Four vitrified and nanowarmed rat kidneys produced urine during 40 minutes of normothermic machine perfusion.
All five bilaterally nephrectomized rats receiving cryobanked, nanowarmed kidney grafts survived 30 days.
results.detail: Renal function normalized after an initial period of graft dysfunction. The study ended at the planned 30-day endpoint.
results.quote: Nanowarmed organs restored renal function and solely sustained the lives of nephrectomized transplant recipients for 30 days post transplant.

results.finding: Eight vitrified and nanowarmed pig kidneys had mean ex vivo creatinine clearance of 4.16 mL/min/100 g.
results.detail: The clearance endpoint averaged measurements at 30 and 60 minutes because perfusate creatinine declined during perfusion.
results.quote:
Creatinine clearance was 4.16 ± 2.79 mL/min/100 g after VNW, 27% 
higher than after CPA exposure alone (3.28 ± 1.80 mL/min/100 g; P = 0.449), but remained 
below 24-h SCS (12.56 ± 6.43; P = 0.001) and fresh controls (18.35 ± 12.50; P = 0.013)

results.finding: Three cryobanked and nanowarmed pig kidney grafts produced urine throughout 120 minutes after transplantation.
results.detail: The graft and remaining native kidney were explanted at the end of observation.
results.quote:
VNW grafts produced urine immediately after reperfusion and sustained urine production 
throughout the 120-min observation period

results.finding: One intact rat heart showed no detectable tissue ice on cryo-μCT at 61 μm resolution.
results.detail: The scan was optimized for detecting cracks and could miss microscopic ice. Figure 4 shows one scanned heart. The total number scanned is unspecified.
results.quote: No crack or ice crystal was observed in the μCT cross sections of the vitrified heart after cooling in sIONP/VS55.

results.finding: One of three vitrified and nanowarmed whole rat hearts responded to electrical pacing.
results.detail: Mean action potential duration was 139.05 ± 2.12 ms in the pacing-responsive nanowarmed heart versus 72.61 ± 7.78 ms in the control comparison.
results.quote: demonstrates that nanowarmed hearts (one out of three) can successfully respond to pacing

results.finding: Whole rat liver tissue showed no detectable ice by cryogenic μCT after cooling to −150 °C (ice-assessment sample size unspecified).
results.detail: Freeze-substitution provided a cellular-level check. Frozen comparison livers showed vascular and intracellular ice.
results.quote: Higher magnification of the section showed no ice crystal formation and hepatocytes (yellow asterisks) with intact nuclei.

results.finding: Whole vitrified and nanowarmed rat livers (n = 3–5 per group) produced bile during 60 minutes of normothermic reperfusion.
results.detail: Function was assessed ex vivo at 37 °C after washout of cryoprotectant and nanoparticles.
results.quote: Overall, bile effluent volumes measured in nanowarmed livers were comparable to CPA-loaded and unloaded livers

results.finding: In 3 whole rabbit kidney vitrification runs, 1 showed apparent freezing of an exposed ureter segment.
results.detail: Table 2 reports that expanding air bubbles under the cover exposed the ureter during cooling. The −123°C glass transition was measured for the vitrification solution.
results.quote: It’s unclear why Kidney 1 recovered poorly, but gas exposure and apparent freezing of the ureter during vitrification and initial gas warming may have been factor.

results.finding: All 3 vitrified and rewarmed rabbit kidneys produced urine acutely after blood reperfusion.
results.quote: All three kidneys produced urine acutely after blood reperfusion before ureter anastomosis during re-implantation in the donor animal.

results.finding: In 3 graft-dependent rabbit recipients, the successful kidney autograft sustained its recipient through 17 months of follow-up.
results.detail: The other two recipients died or were euthanized within three days.
results.quote: The recipient of Kidney 2 completely recovered and survived long-term with all measured clinical parameters returning to normal values and remaining clinically normal 17 months after transplantation

results.finding: Rabbit recipients of rewarmed, vitrified kidney allografts (sample size unstated) survived at least 4 days.
results.detail: The institute release attributes the findings to a peer-reviewed Matter paper.
